title: Properties of Media & Preparing Products for Distribution
description: How image resolution, colour depth, compression and bitrate affect quality and file size when optimising media products.
content_html:
Why Properties Matter

Every media file has technical properties that determine its visual or audio quality and its file size. Understanding these properties is essential because file size and quality always exist in tension: higher quality means larger files, and larger files take longer to download, stream or load. A media creator must balance these properties for the specific platform and audience. A print-quality photograph that is perfect in a magazine will be far too large for a web page, where a viewer expects the page to load in under two seconds. Preparing a product for distribution means making deliberate decisions about each technical property to optimise the file for its purpose.

Image Resolution and Dimensions

Resolution describes how much detail an image contains. For print, resolution is measured in dots per inch (DPI): professional print output requires at least 300 DPI, and images printed at lower resolutions appear blurry or pixelated. For screen display (websites, presentations, social media), 72 to 96 pixels per inch (PPI) is sufficient because monitors display fewer pixels per physical inch than a printer lays down ink dots. Sending a 300 DPI image to a website is wasteful — it produces an unnecessarily large file with no visible quality benefit to the viewer.

Dimensions are measured in pixels (width x height). A full-width website banner might need to be 1920 x 1080 pixels, while a social media profile picture might only need to be 400 x 400 pixels. Resizing an image to the exact dimensions required for the platform reduces file size without the need for aggressive compression. As a rule, always reduce image dimensions before uploading to a web platform, rather than relying on the platform to resize the image for you.

Key Fact

Print images require at least 300 DPI (dots per inch) to appear sharp. Screen images require only 72 to 96 PPI (pixels per inch) because monitor displays do not resolve detail as finely as printed ink. Using a 300 DPI image on a website wastes bandwidth without improving the viewer's experience.

Bit Depth and Colour

Bit depth determines how many colours an image can contain. A 1-bit image contains only black and white (2 colours). An 8-bit image can contain 256 colours — enough for simple graphics and GIF animations, but not for photographs. A 24-bit image uses 8 bits per channel across three channels (red, green, blue), giving over 16 million possible colours — this is referred to as true colour and is the standard for photographs and complex digital artwork. A 32-bit image adds an alpha channel for transparency information on top of the 24-bit colour data. Higher bit depth produces better colour accuracy but increases file size.

GIF files are limited to an 8-bit palette of 256 colours. This is why GIFs look flat or banded when used for photographs — the limited palette cannot accurately represent the millions of subtle tones in a photo. GIF is best reserved for simple graphics, text-based animations and logos where only a few colours are needed. PNG supports both 8-bit (PNG-8) and 24-bit (PNG-24) colour. PNG-8 produces smaller files than PNG-24 but with the same 256-colour limit as GIF; PNG-24 supports full true colour and is appropriate for photographs needing transparency. Choosing between PNG-8 and PNG-24 is itself a file size vs quality decision that a creator must make based on the complexity of the image.

Compression: Lossy vs Lossless

Compression is the process of reducing a file's size so it can be stored, transferred or streamed more efficiently. Lossy compression permanently removes data that the human eye or ear is least likely to notice, producing a significantly smaller file at the cost of some quality. JPEG and MP3 are lossy formats. Lossless compression encodes the data more efficiently without discarding anything, so the original can be perfectly reconstructed. PNG, GIF and WAV are lossless. The choice between lossy and lossless depends on the purpose: professional editing and print require lossless quality; web delivery and streaming benefit from the smaller file sizes that lossy compression provides.

Each time a JPEG image is opened, edited and re-saved, another round of lossy compression is applied. The quality loss accumulates with every save, a phenomenon sometimes called generation loss. After several cycles, visible artefacts appear: blocky patterns around edges, smearing in areas of fine detail, and washed-out colours. This is why professional photographers and designers always keep the original high-resolution RAW or TIFF file and export a JPEG only at the very end of the editing process — never editing from the JPEG directly. The same principle applies to audio: always keep the original WAV or uncompressed source file and export the MP3 as the final delivery format.

Bitrate for Audio and Video

Bitrate is the amount of data used per second of audio or video playback, measured in kilobits per second (kbps) or megabits per second (Mbps). For audio, a bitrate of 128 kbps is considered acceptable for casual listening; 320 kbps is considered high quality for MP3. For video, a bitrate of 5 to 8 Mbps is typical for 1080p HD streaming; 4K video may require 35 to 45 Mbps or more. Higher bitrate produces better quality but larger files that require more bandwidth to stream. A video intended for social media upload will be exported at a lower bitrate than the same video destined for a cinema screen or broadcast.

Key Fact

Bitrate directly controls the trade-off between quality and file size for audio and video. Standard MP3 bitrates range from 128 kbps (acceptable quality) to 320 kbps (high quality). Standard video bitrates for web delivery range from 1 Mbps (low quality, small file) to 8 Mbps or more for 1080p HD. Higher bitrate files require faster internet connections to stream without buffering.
exam_tip_html: Questions about properties often ask you to ‘justify’ a choice — which means you must explain why a particular value or format was chosen, not just name it. For DPI, always link the number to the output: 300 DPI because it is going to print; 72 PPI because it is for the web. For compression, always state whether it is lossy or lossless and why that matters for the purpose. For bitrate, always mention the quality-versus-file-size trade-off. These justification chains are what separate Secure from Mastering answers.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Print images require at least 300 DPI; screen images require 72 to 96 PPI; using a higher resolution than needed wastes file size without improving quality for the viewer.
  • Bit depth determines how many colours an image can contain: 8-bit supports 256 colours; 24-bit supports over 16 million (true colour). Higher bit depth increases file size.
  • Lossy compression (JPEG, MP3) permanently removes data to reduce file size; lossless compression (PNG, WAV) reduces size without losing data. Bitrate controls the data-per-second in audio and video, directly trading quality for file size.

glossary_terms.definition: The number of pixels per inch (PPI) or dots per inch (DPI) in an image, which determines how sharp it appears at a given print size. Screen resolution is typically 72-96 PPI; print requires at least 300 DPI.
The number of bits used to represent the colour of each pixel in an image. An 8-bit image can display 256 colours; a 24-bit image can display over 16 million colours (true colour).
A method of reducing the size of a media file either by permanently discarding data (lossy) or by encoding data more efficiently without discarding any (lossless).
The amount of data processed per second in an audio or video file, measured in kilobits per second (kbps) or megabits per second (Mbps). Higher bitrate means higher quality and larger files.

practice_questions.text:
What is the minimum recommended resolution for an image that will be printed in a professional publication?
A) 72 DPI
B) 150 DPI
C) 300 DPI
D) 600 PPI
State two technical properties of a digital image that affect its file size.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: resolution (DPI/PPI); dimensions (pixel width and height); bit depth / colour depth; compression type (lossy or lossless); file format. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by lossy compression and give one disadvantage of using it.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. Simple point (1 mark): e.g. 'lossy compression removes some data'. Development (2 marks): e.g. 'lossy compression permanently removes data that is judged least noticeable, reducing file size at the cost of some quality that cannot be recovered'. Disadvantage with further development (3 marks): e.g. 'one disadvantage is generation loss: each time a JPEG is re-saved, another round of compression is applied, and the cumulative quality loss produces visible artefacts such as blockiness around edges after several edits'. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what bit depth means in the context of a digital image, and give one example of how different bit depths are used in practice.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): bit depth is the number of bits used to represent the colour of each pixel; a higher bit depth means more possible colours and therefore more accurate colour representation, but a larger file size (2 marks for a developed description covering number of colours and the quality/size trade-off; 1 mark for a basic statement). Example (up to 2 marks): an 8-bit image can display 256 colours and is suitable for a simple logo or GIF animation; a 24-bit image (true colour) can display over 16 million colours and is used for photographs where subtle colour gradations must be preserved accurately (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for one example only or a vague description). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A student has created a 10-minute video for a school website. The exported file is 4 GB and takes over three minutes to load. The student needs to reduce the file size while keeping the quality acceptable for web streaming.

Discuss the technical changes the student could make to reduce the file size without significantly affecting the viewer's experience.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two relevant technical changes with justification: reducing the bitrate (e.g. from a broadcast-quality 50 Mbps to a web-appropriate 5-8 Mbps for 1080p) eliminates most of the file size; reducing the output resolution from 4K to 1080p would also significantly reduce size with no visible difference on a standard school monitor; using H.264 encoding in an MP4 container applies efficient lossy compression appropriate for web delivery. Acknowledges the trade-off: too low a bitrate produces visible artefacts and buffering. Applied to the school-website scenario. Secure (3-4 marks): At least two changes identified and briefly justified. Developing (2 marks): One change identified, limited justification. Emerging (1 mark): A single point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A graphic designer is preparing a set of images for both a printed brochure and a company website. The same photograph will appear in both publications.

Evaluate the decisions the designer should make about resolution, file format and compression for each version of the image, and justify why the two versions must be prepared differently.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8 marks): A sustained evaluation covering all three properties for each output. Print version: 300 DPI; TIFF or high-quality JPEG (minimal or no compression); larger file size is acceptable because the file is sent directly to the printer, not downloaded by a viewer. Web version: 72-96 PPI; JPEG with moderate lossy compression; dimensions reduced to the exact display size (e.g. 1200 x 800 px); small file size is essential so the page loads quickly. Justification for the difference: the viewer's experience differs — a print reader holds the image at close range and notices low resolution, whereas a web viewer on a standard monitor cannot distinguish a 72 PPI image from a 300 PPI image but will notice slow loading times. A clear judgement is reached that the different purposes require genuinely different technical specifications, not simply ‘one is better than the other’. Secure (5-6 marks): Both versions addressed with correct properties and some justification. Developing (3-4 marks): Surface-level description of one or both versions. Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What is the minimum recommended DPI for an image that will be used in a professionally printed document?
A 24-bit image is described as 'true colour'. Approximately how many colours can it display?
JPEG uses _____ compression, which permanently removes data from the image to reduce file size.
Bitrate is measured in kilobits per second (kbps) or megabits per second (Mbps) and determines the trade-off between audio/video _____ and file size.
Match each property to the correct description of how it affects a media file.
right: The amount of data per second in audio or video, controlling quality and file size
The sharpness of an image at a given physical size, measured as dots or pixels per inch
The number of colours available per pixel; higher values improve colour accuracy

flashcard_questions.q: What DPI is recommended as the minimum for professional print output?
What PPI is sufficient for images displayed on a website?
How many colours can an 8-bit image display?
What is true colour and how many bits does it use?
flashcard_questions.a: True colour is 24-bit, displaying over 16 million colours.
Compression that permanently discards data to reduce file size, at a cost to quality.
Compression that reduces file size without discarding any data, so quality is perfectly preserved.

flashcard_questions.q: Why should a JPEG file not be re-saved multiple times during editing?
flashcard_questions.a: Each save applies another round of lossy compression, causing cumulative quality loss.

flashcard_questions.q: What unit is bitrate measured in for audio files?
What bitrate is considered high quality for an MP3 audio file?
Why does a print image need a higher DPI than a screen image?
flashcard_questions.a: Printers lay down more ink dots per inch than a monitor displays pixels, so more detail is needed for a sharp print.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a 32-bit image include that a 24-bit image does not?
flashcard_questions.a: An alpha channel for transparency information.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the trade-off when increasing the bitrate of a video?
flashcard_questions.a: Higher quality but a larger file size that requires more bandwidth to stream.
